name: Seismic Moment
description: Computes the seismic moment of an earthquake, a physical measure of its size, as the product of the crustal shear modulus mu, the rupture area A, and the average fault slip D. Larger rupture area or slip yields a proportionally larger moment.
notes: Use SI units (Pa, m², m) to get moment in newton-metres. Seismic moment scales linearly with area and slip, unlike magnitude which is logarithmic.

name: Seismic Energy (Gutenberg-Richter)
description: Estimates the radiated seismic energy of an earthquake from its magnitude M using the Gutenberg-Richter energy relation 10^(4.8 + 1.5·M). Energy rises by a factor of about 32 for each unit increase in magnitude.
notes: M is the dimensionless magnitude and the result is in joules. This is an empirical estimate of radiated energy and differs from the moment-based magnitude definition.

name: Stress Drop (circular fault)
description: Estimates the static stress drop of an earthquake on a circular fault from its seismic moment M0 and fault radius r, using the Eshelby relation (7/16)*M0/r^3. The result, in pascals, measures how much shear stress was released along the rupture.
notes: Assumes a circular crack in a uniform elastic medium. Because it scales as 1/r^3, small errors in the radius strongly affect the result; typical crustal earthquakes give a few MPa.

name: Brune Corner Frequency
description: Computes the corner frequency of an earthquake source spectrum from the S-wave velocity Vs and source radius r using Brune's model, fc = 0.37*Vs/r. The corner frequency marks where the displacement spectrum begins to fall off and reflects source size.
notes: Larger sources give lower corner frequencies. The 0.37 constant is specific to Brune's circular source model; other models use different coefficients, so values are model-dependent.

name: Source Radius (Brune)
description: Inverts Brune's model to estimate the earthquake source radius from the S-wave velocity Vs and the observed corner frequency fc, as r = 0.37*Vs/fc. Lower corner frequencies imply larger rupture areas.
notes: The inverse of the corner-frequency relation; uses the same 0.37 Brune constant. Corner frequency must come from the S-wave spectrum for consistency, and results are sensitive to how fc is picked.

name: Distance from S-P Time
description: Estimates the distance to an earthquake source from the S-minus-P arrival time difference dt and the P- and S-wave velocities, as dt*Vp*Vs/(Vp - Vs). The later-arriving S wave lags the P wave more with distance.
notes: Assumes a straight ray path through a uniform-velocity medium, so it is an approximation for shallow, nearby events. Requires Vp greater than Vs; result is a hypocentral distance.

name: Omori-Utsu Aftershock Rate
description: Gives the rate of aftershocks per day at time t after a mainshock using the modified Omori (Omori-Utsu) law, K/(c + t)^p. Aftershock frequency decays with time governed by the productivity K, time offset c, and exponent p.
notes: Time t and offset c are in days; the rate is per day. The exponent p is typically near 1, and c prevents the singularity at t = 0 shortly after the mainshock.

name: Gutenberg-Richter Frequency
description: Computes the number of earthquakes with magnitude at least M from the Gutenberg-Richter relation, 10^(a - b*M). The a-value sets overall seismicity and the b-value sets how quickly frequency drops with increasing magnitude.
notes: Gives cumulative frequency (events of magnitude M or greater), typically over a set time and region embedded in a. A b-value near 1 means each unit magnitude increase makes events about ten times rarer.

name: Local Magnitude (Southern California)
description: Calculates Richter local magnitude ML from a Wood-Anderson seismograph amplitude A and epicentral distance D using the Southern California calibration, log(A) + 1.11*log(D) + 0.00189*D - 2.09. The distance terms correct for wave attenuation.
notes: Amplitude A is in mm on a Wood-Anderson instrument and distance D in km; log is base-10. The coefficients are calibrated for Southern California and are not universal.

name: Body-Wave Magnitude
description: Determines the body-wave magnitude mb from the ground-motion amplitude A, its period T, and a distance-depth calibration term Q, as log(A/T) + Q. It uses the amplitude-to-period ratio of teleseismic P waves.
notes: Amplitude A is in micrometres and period T in seconds; Q depends on distance and focal depth from standard tables. mb tends to saturate for very large earthquakes.

name: Surface-Wave Magnitude
description: Computes the surface-wave magnitude Ms from the ground amplitude A, period T, and epicentral distance D using log(A/T) + 1.66*log(D) + 3.3. It is based on long-period Rayleigh waves around 20 s period.
notes: Amplitude A is in micrometres, period T in seconds, and distance D in degrees. The formula is intended for shallow events and standard around T near 20 s; deep earthquakes are underestimated.

name: PGA Attenuation (simplified)
description: Estimates peak ground acceleration in g from a simplified attenuation (ground-motion) relation, a*exp(b*M)/R^c, where magnitude M raises PGA exponentially and distance R reduces it by geometric spreading with exponent c.
notes: The coefficients a, b, c are empirical and region-specific placeholders, not universal values. Real ground-motion models add saturation, site, and depth terms; this is a schematic form only.

name: Rupture Length (Wells-Coppersmith)
description: Estimates the surface rupture length of a fault in kilometres from earthquake magnitude M using the Wells and Coppersmith empirical regression, 10^(-3.22+0.69*M). Larger magnitudes correspond to longer ruptures.
notes: Empirical relation from a global dataset; coefficients here are for all fault types and give a mean estimate with real scatter. Result is surface rupture length in km, not subsurface rupture.

name: Rupture Area (Wells-Coppersmith)
description: Estimates the rupture area of a fault in square kilometres from earthquake magnitude M using the Wells and Coppersmith regression, 10^(-3.49+0.91*M). Rupture area grows rapidly with magnitude.
notes: Empirical mean relation with real scatter; coefficients are for all fault types combined. Output is subsurface rupture area in km^2, useful for fault source characterization.

name: Average Slip (Wells-Coppersmith)
description: Estimates the average coseismic slip on a fault in metres from earthquake magnitude M using the Wells and Coppersmith regression, 10^(-4.80+0.69*M). It gives the mean displacement across the rupture surface.
notes: Empirical mean with substantial scatter; represents average, not maximum, slip. Coefficients combine all fault types and should not be treated as exact for a single event.

name: Earthquake Recurrence Interval
description: Computes the average recurrence interval between large earthquakes on a fault as the coseismic slip D divided by the long-term slip rate s. It is the time needed to reaccumulate the slip released in one event.
notes: Slip D is in metres and slip rate s in metres per year, giving years. Assumes a characteristic-earthquake model where each event releases the same slip at a steady rate.

name: Seismic Moment Rate
description: Computes the rate at which seismic moment accumulates on a fault from the shear modulus mu, fault area A, and slip rate sr, as mu*A*sr. It quantifies how fast tectonic loading builds up moment available for future earthquakes.
notes: Uses SI units: mu in Pa, area in m^2, slip rate in m/yr, giving N·m per year. Represents the geodetic moment budget, which released seismicity should balance over time.

name: Energy Magnitude
description: Converts the radiated seismic energy En in joules into an energy magnitude Me using the Choy-Boatwright relation, (2/3)*(log(En) - 4.4). It expresses the earthquake's radiated energy on the magnitude scale.
notes: Energy En is in joules and log is base-10. Energy magnitude reflects radiated energy and can differ from moment magnitude, which reflects static fault displacement.

name: Rupture Duration
description: Estimates the time an earthquake rupture takes to propagate along a fault as the rupture length L divided by the rupture velocity Vr. It gives an order-of-magnitude duration of the faulting process.
notes: Length L is in metres and rupture velocity Vr in metres per second, giving seconds. Assumes unilateral rupture at constant speed; typical Vr is 70-90 percent of the shear-wave velocity.

name: Anelastic Attenuation (amplitude)
description: Gives the seismic wave amplitude after geometric spreading and anelastic attenuation, A0/R*exp(-pi*f*R/(Q*V)). The 1/R term is spreading and the exponential term is energy loss governed by the quality factor Q.
notes: Distance R and velocity V in SI, frequency f in Hz; the dimensionless Q measures how little energy is lost per cycle. Higher frequencies and lower Q attenuate faster.

name: Instrumental Intensity (Wald)
description: Estimates the instrumental Modified Mercalli Intensity from peak ground acceleration using Wald et al.'s regression, 3.66*log(PGA) - 1.66. It maps recorded shaking onto the felt-intensity scale.
notes: PGA is in cm/s^2 (gal) and log is base-10. Valid roughly for intensities V-VIII; at low and very high intensities velocity-based relations are used instead.

name: Fault Slip from Stress Drop
description: Estimates the average fault slip from the stress drop ds, a characteristic fault dimension L, and the shear modulus mu, as ds*L/mu. Slip scales with how much stress was released over the rupture size.
notes: All quantities in SI: stress drop and shear modulus in Pa, dimension in m, giving slip in metres. This is a scaling relation with an order-unity geometric factor omitted.

name: b-value (Aki-Utsu)
description: Estimates the Gutenberg-Richter b-value using the Aki-Utsu maximum-likelihood formula, log(e)/(Mmean - Mmin), from the mean magnitude and the minimum (completeness) magnitude of a catalog.
notes: log(e) is the base-10 log of Euler's number (about 0.4343); magnitudes are dimensionless. The minimum magnitude must be the catalog completeness threshold for the estimate to be unbiased.

name: Duration Magnitude
description: Computes a coda duration magnitude Md from the signal duration and epicentral distance using a + b*log(dur) + c*D. It uses how long the earthquake coda lasts instead of peak amplitude.
notes: Duration is in seconds, distance D in km, and log is base-10; coefficients a, b, c are network-specific calibrations. Useful for small local events where amplitude clips or saturates.
